extracted.intended_audience: scholars, historians, philosophers, and educated readers interested in standards for writing and evaluating history, poesy, and natural philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting standards and guidance for composing and judging works of history, biography, poetry (poesy), ecclesiastical history, and natural philosophy as presented in an early-modern treatise. Emphasises sources, scope, method, and the separation of genres and enquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor person-focused narratives for truer representation
rubrics_metrics.description: A history or narration that propounds a person to represent, in whom actions (public and private) commingle, will of necessity contain a more true, native, and lively representation than histories of times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer biographies and relations of particular actions (wars, expeditions, conspiracies) when accuracy and purity of account are required; these allow choice of an argument comprehensible within the writer's knowledge. By contrast, broad histories of long periods inherit many blanks which must be filled by the writer's wit and conjecture, reducing certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope to what the writer can comprehend and observe
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer undertaking the story of a long time cannot but meet with many blanks and spaces which he must be forced to fill up out of his own wit and conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, choose arguments and temporal scopes that lie within the writer's notice and instructions to avoid speculative filling-in; prefer narrower, well-evidenced narratives to sweeping chronologies when truthfulness is a goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve classical/historical texts intact when continuing sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In sequences of story (e.g., Greece and Rome) the texts of Thucydides, Xenophon, Livy, Polybius, Sallust, Caesar, Appian, Tacitus, Herodian should be kept entire, without any diminution at all, and only to be supplied and continued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not excise or diminish the canonical text; continue and supply where necessary rather than edit out; treating ancient authorities as a continuous foundation is a mark of good historical practice (a matter of magnificence rather than supererogation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose unified national histories after political union; choose manageable periods
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be an honourable and memorable work if Great Britain, now joined in monarchy, were joined in one history for the times passed; if that seems too great, choose a smaller compass, e.g., from the uniting of the Roses to the uniting of the kingdoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When national or political unifications occur, consider composing a single history to reflect the new political unit; if the whole period is unwieldy, select a bounded, eventful epoch that offers rich variety and manageable scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write more lives (biographies) of worthy personages
rubrics_metrics.description: The times have so little esteemed the virtues of the times that writings of lives are not frequent; many worthy personages deserve better than dispersed report or barren eulogies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase production of biographies ('lives') to preserve memory and virtue; specific, focused lives enrich larger histories and counteract neglect of deserving individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect particular actions and use diaries/journals as primary source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularity of actions memorable, if tolerably reported as they pass, will help in compiling a complete history later; keeping journals is a use well received in memorable enterprises such as wars, navigations, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage contemporaneous recording (journals, diaries) of events, daily particulars, and actions of enterprises; treat these collections as a 'nursery garden' from which future historians can plant full histories when a fitting writer arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish annals (state matters) from journals (acts and accidents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tacitus's partition: annals are appropriated to matters of estate and journals to acts and accidents of a meaner nature; nothing derogates the dignity of a state more than confusion of degrees, nor does it little imbase the authority of a history to intermingle matters of triumph, ceremony, or novelty with matters of state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep formal state annals separate from quotidian journals and avoid mixing ceremonial or novel occurrences with the core matters of state; maintain proper degrees and categorisation to preserve historical dignity and authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve political/observational discourse separate from narrative history
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a form of writing containing a scattered history of actions with politic discourse and observation, not incorporated into the history but separately; it is more fit among books of policy than among books of history. It is the true office of history to represent events and leave observations and conclusions to each reader's judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid mixing extended political commentary and prescriptive observations inside narrative history; if the intention is policy or ruminated discourse, classify and publish it as political treatise rather than as history to keep genres clear and histories impartial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use letters, orations, and apophthegms as crucial historical appendices and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of words only—orations, letters, brief speeches or sayings—are appropriate to custody and receipt of words; letters from wise men are among all the words of man the best for history, and letters of actors are the best instructions for history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve, collect, and consult private correspondence, public orations, and memorable sayings as primary evidence; favour letters and dispatches from those who managed or were privy to affairs, and value apophthegms composed by the principal actors where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise divisions of poesy and employ each according to purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Poesy is feigned history and divides into narrative (imitation of history), representative (visible history), and allusive/parabolical (narration applied to express a special purpose). Poesy serves magnanimity, morality, and delectation and participates in elevating the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the poetic mode to fit the intent: narrative for heroic/chronicle-like tales, representative for stage and spectacle, allusive for moral or instructive purposes. Use poesy to magnify virtues and for moral and aesthetic elevation, understanding its licence compared to strict history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parables and fables with discernment; avoid forced allegorical exegesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Parabolical poesy may be used to demonstrate or to retire/obscure secrets; although exposition of fables sometimes has felicity, assigning deep inward meanings to ancient poets (e.g., imposing Stoic or allegorical meanings) is often a corruption — better to avoid insisting a fable originally bore the moral assigned to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting or employing fables and parables, do so with caution; do not invent retroactive, strained moral meanings without evidence. Beware of commentators who force philosophical systems onto poets' fictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: In ecclesiastical history, pair prophecies with their fulfillments carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: History of prophecy consists of prophecy and the accomplishment; the nature of such a work ought to sort every prophecy of Scripture with the event fulfilling the same throughout the ages, for the confirmation of faith and illumination of the Church, while allowing the latitude proper to divine prophecies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile prophetic texts alongside their historical fulfillments across ages; do the work with wisdom, sobriety, and reverence, mindful that fulfillments may be springing and germinant over many ages rather than punctual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record history of Providence as notable examples of God's judgments and deliverances
rubrics_metrics.description: History of Providence contains the correspondence between God's revealed will and His secret will; at times God writes His will in such legible examples that 'he that runneth by may read it' — notable events of judgments, chastisements, deliverances, and blessings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and present notable events and examples that show providential patterns; this work has been undertaken by many and is appropriate for strengthening faith and illustrating moral lessons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a philosophia prima (summary or universal philosophy) to gather common axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Before special parts of philosophy, erect one universal science, philosophia prima, as a receptacle for all profitable observations and axioms that fall not within any special part of philosophy — common principles that are useful across disciplines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create and maintain a domain for general axioms and cross-disciplinary rules (e.g., rules about equality, proportion, change) that inform justice, mathematics, rhetoric, and other arts; use it to abridge and unite knowledge not confined to one branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide natural philosophy into speculative (inquisition of causes) and operative (production of effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural philosophy should be divided into the inquisition of causes (speculative, natural science/theory) and the production of effects (operative, natural prudence). Some practitioners should dig (pioneers/inquirers), others refine and hammer (experimenters/technicians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organise natural philosophers into those who seek causes from experiments and those who translate causes into new operations and works. Promote both ascendent method (experiments to causes) and descendent method (causes to inventions), and revive the correct sense of 'natural magic' as natural prudence, purged of superstition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt an experimental method: ascend from experiments to causes and descend from causes to experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: True natural philosophy has a double ladder: ascending from experiments to invention of causes, and descending from causes to invention of new experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure inquiry so experiments inform causal hypotheses, and causal understanding drives new experimental invention; this iterative cycle is essential for fruitful natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep theology and natural philosophy distinct: do not use nature to determine mysteries of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine philosophy or natural theology suffices to convince atheism but does not inform religion; it is not safe to use contemplation of nature to induce verities of points of faith — 'Da fidei quæ fidei sunt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attempting to prove or reduce matters of revealed religion to natural philosophy; reserve theological mysteries to proper theological methods and treat natural theology as limited in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries into angels/spirits allowed but avoid adoration and fantastical opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: While Scripture forbids pressing into worship of angels or fantastical claims about them, sober and grounded inquiry into their nature, power, illusions, or stratagems (as far as Scripture or reason allows) is not interdicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit scholarly inquiry into spiritual beings' nature and effects, but avoid adoration, baseless exaltation of knowledge, or fantastical speculation; treat such inquiries as part of spiritual wisdom when properly grounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect antiquity in terminology and avoid gratuitous innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain ancient terms and respect antiquity 'usque ad aras'; although uses and definitions may be altered moderately, coming in 'in one's own name' (i.e., inventing new terms and overturning antiquity) is not a good sign of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer continuity with established terminology and doctrines unless change is justified by truth or proficience; avoid rhetorical innovation for its own sake and be cautious about overturning ancient wisdom without sound reasons.
